title: The ECB traces how AI and sovereign losses could reach the same balance sheets
summary: The ECB’s November Financial Stability Review identifies a risk that an equity correction, a sovereign bond sell-off and pressure on short-term funding could reinforce one another. Euro area banks entered this period profitable and well capitalised. The more immediate vulnerability lay with investors financing concentrated positions with leverage or promising redemptions against less liquid assets. Links between those investors and banks make losses outside the banking sector relevant to the availability of credit inside it. The Review presents this as a possible sequence of events. It does not predict a simultaneous crash (overview, Charts 2–4).

Economic conditions had held up better than markets expected between July and October. Euro area GDP rose 0.4% in the third quarter. Consumption and public investment supported activity, while releases from strategic petroleum reserves cushioned the energy shock. Neither the upside surprises nor the temporary cushion resolved the underlying supply disruption. Expensive energy and trade barriers could squeeze the same firms already facing higher borrowing costs. Weaker corporate cash flow and hiring would then expose households, particularly those with low incomes and little capacity to absorb another increase in living costs. Residential property trends differed markedly by country. The aggregate offered little guidance for calibrating local borrower safeguards (Chapter 1 and Box 1).

The financing of AI investment had changed. Internal profits initially covered much of the build-out. The Review reports that for most large cloud providers free cash flow had declined significantly since early 2025, turned negative in 2026 and was expected to remain negative until 2028. Bonds, equity issuance, leasing and financing outside the providers’ own balance sheets increasingly spread the risk to other investors. A chipmaker or cloud provider can finance a customer that then commits to buying its services. Observed bookings can consequently rise without establishing how much independent end-user cash will ultimately pay for the infrastructure. Productivity gains for the economy and returns to the firms financing its build-out could diverge (Section 2.3 and Boxes 3–4).

A dividend discount decomposition attributes much of the equity advance to expectations of earnings growth. Its risk-premium contribution is a model residual. It measures neither investor flows nor an observed insurance premium. Concentration was also appearing in credit. Big technology issuers still represented a modest share of the overall euro investment-grade benchmark, but their long maturities made them more prominent at the long end. Non-banks’ holdings in US technology and AI-related firms accounted for 16% to 26% of their equity investments across the groups considered, partly because existing holdings had appreciated. Large IPOs could further change benchmark exposure, although historical associations between heavy issuance and subsequent returns do not establish a causal timing signal (Chart 2, Box 4, Section 4.1 and Special Feature C).

Sovereign financing needs provide a second source of stress. Roughly a quarter of outstanding euro area sovereign debt was due before the end of 2028. Long yields had risen, while more price-sensitive investors were absorbing supply. Hedge funds’ financed positions can make markets more liquid in ordinary conditions. When prices fall or financing terms tighten, reducing those positions can instead amplify the move. Shorter-dated purchases by non-banks provide no assurance of equivalent demand for new long bonds. Higher sovereign yields could raise corporate refinancing costs at the same time as AI firms seek financing (Section 2.2, Chapter 4 and Box 7).

Euro area banks’ aggregate non-performing loan ratio reached a record low of 2.2% in September. Available loan data identified €24.3 billion in bank commitments to 165 important AI supply-chain firms and their subsidiaries through June, including €11 billion undrawn. Some exposures booked outside the euro area were absent. Banks also lend to funds and depend on non-banks for funding. A fund facing margin calls might withdraw money from a bank just as that bank reduces the fund’s credit line. The ECB favours preserving releasable bank capital buffers and borrower-based measures, alongside better alignment of fund redemption terms with asset liquidity, stronger margin preparedness and cross-border monitoring of leveraged positions. Its special features also flag concentrated technology providers as a possible common source of operational losses (Sections 3.3–3.5 and 4.4).

questions.question: How much end-user revenue can support the new AI debt?
questions.detail: The Review identifies supplier financing, purchase commitments and off-balance-sheet obligations, but available accounts do not establish how much demand originates outside the financing network. Compare the company filings cited in Box 3 with lease commitments, cash collections and the maturity of debt and guarantees. These distinctions matter more for creditors’ recovery prospects than aggregate industry revenue growth alone.

questions.question: Which investors would have to sell sovereign bonds if short-term financing tightened?
questions.detail: Box 7 identifies hedge fund participation in euro repo markets, while the sovereign chapter documents substantial refinancing needs. The scale of forced selling depends on maturity mismatches, collateral terms and available cash. Examine the repo transaction and holdings data underlying the Review alongside national issuance calendars, distinguishing net demand for long-duration paper from short-dated purchases.

questions.question: Could bank funding withdrawals coincide with drawdowns on committed credit lines?
questions.detail: A fund under pressure can withdraw a bank deposit and need more credit at the same time. Aggregate direct lending to the AI supply chain covers only part of that exposure. Compare the Review’s supervisory loan and securities holdings data by counterparty, including undrawn commitments, withdrawal terms and cross-border booking. A concentration among the same funds and banks would matter more for liquidity than the aggregate loan share.
